subsection: 1. Concepts of work and attitudes to work

notes.b: Work is any activity that produces goods or services, using a person's time and effort. It is not only paid: it falls into three types, which differ in whether it is paid, who it is for and whether it is chosen.
points: Paid employment is work done for financial gain (a wage, salary, fees or profit), usually under a contract of employment between employer and employee. It may be permanent, temporary, full-time, part-time or contract-based.

Self-employment is also paid work, not a fourth type: the worker earns income directly from their own trade, business or profession and carries the financial risk, because there is no employer to pay them if business is poor.
Paid employment carries entitlement to PRSI-based social insurance (cover built up through PRSI contributions) and, in many jobs, a pension, sick pay and paid holidays.

Unpaid work in the home is done without financial reward, mainly for the household: housework, cooking, cleaning, laundry, shopping, child care and care of elderly or disabled relatives. It is done out of duty or family commitment.
Home-related activities such as DIY, home maintenance, gardening and household budgeting are also unpaid work, because they keep the home running without anyone being paid.

Voluntary work is unpaid work done freely, by choice, for people or causes outside the household, usually through a charity, community group or organisation, to help others and improve the community. Volunteers may receive expenses but no wage.
Examples of voluntary work include St Vincent de Paul, charity shops, fundraising and helping at local sports clubs.

In one line each: paid work brings income; unpaid work in the home is a household duty with no income; voluntary work is chosen, for the wider community, with no income. Work placements and work experience are unpaid but are not the same as voluntary work.

The distinction matters because paid work brings income and entitlements, while unpaid and voluntary work are not counted in earnings. They still use a person's time, which is also a resource, so work affects the time and money available for family life.
notes.tip: When asked to explain or differentiate the three types, give one clear point and one example for each: paid (wage, contract, benefits), unpaid (housework, care, DIY) and voluntary (charity, free choice, community). Say clearly that unpaid work in the home is a household duty, whereas voluntary work is a free choice for people outside the household.

notes.b: Job satisfaction is how fulfilled and content a person is in their work. It comes from two sources: rewards that surround the job (extrinsic) and the task itself (intrinsic). A worker usually gets a mix of both, and occupations differ in the balance.
points: Extrinsic satisfaction comes from rewards linked to the job rather than from the task itself. Sources are pay, bonuses, pension, paid holidays and leave, job security, promotion prospects, working conditions, and company benefits such as a car or private health insurance.
Repetitive, uninteresting work, such as assembly-line production, may leave pay as the main source of satisfaction, because the worker works 'for the money'.
Satisfaction is also gained by spending income on goods, leisure and socialising outside work.
Extrinsic rewards can sustain a worker in a job, but on their own they bring less pride and self-esteem, because they do not come from the work itself.

Intrinsic satisfaction comes from the work itself: the fulfilment, pleasure and creativity it offers. Sources are challenge and variety in tasks, autonomy and responsibility, the chance to use skills, pride in a finished task, achievement and feeling useful.
Work builds self-esteem, confidence and independence.
Work can confer status and respect in the community and a personal identity, such as being a nurse or a teacher, which meets social and psychological needs.
Intrinsic satisfaction is strongest when a job matches a person's skills and interests, because the worker enjoys and takes pride in what they do.
notes.tip: Extrinsic means rewards outside the task and intrinsic means from the task itself. Do not reverse them, and never call pay intrinsic. For an analysis question, define each, give examples, say how each shapes motivation, pride and loyalty, and say that a mix is typical.

notes.b: Work ethic is the attitude a person brings to work. Work attainment is about getting and achieving the kind of work a person is aiming for.
points: Work ethic is a person's commitment to working hard and doing a job well. It is shown through punctuality, good attendance and low absenteeism, reliability, effort, honesty, commitment to tasks, pride in the work, and respect for authority, colleagues and employer.
Employers value a strong work ethic, and it helps a worker to keep a job, be promoted and get good references. A positive attitude makes a worker more likely to be trusted with responsibility.
Work ethic is influenced by upbringing, education and the example of family and peers.

Work attainment is getting and achieving the kind of work a person wants. How far someone attains the work they aim for is affected by education and qualifications, social group, ambition and aspirations, family expectations, and the availability of jobs.
People who have high aspirations (goals they set themselves) and are encouraged at home are more likely to attain work in a desired field.
notes.tip: Do not define work attainment as promotion. It means getting the work a person is aiming for, shaped by education, social group, aspirations and opportunity. Promotion is a result of a good work ethic.

notes.h: Factors that shape attitudes to work
notes.b: A person's attitude to work, positive or negative, is shaped by their background, their circumstances and what the job is like. Each factor can raise or lower how a worker feels about their job.
points: Upbringing and family attitudes to work, together with education and qualifications and earlier work experience, shape expectations before a person starts a job.

Social group, ambition and economic situation: children from higher socio-economic groups tend to have higher educational aspirations and long-term goals, and a person's financial situation affects how much they need the job.
Financial reward: fair pay and benefits encourage a positive attitude, while poor pay discourages it.
Fulfilment and personal identity: some occupations confer status in the community, which can encourage a positive attitude to work, and a worker who feels fulfilled has higher self-esteem.
Social contact: a workplace meets social needs through friendships, and peer pressure influences how seriously a worker takes the job.

Working environment and conditions: a good atmosphere and a supportive supervisor produce a positive attitude, whereas poor conditions, a long commute and unsociable hours produce a negative one. Part-time work, job-sharing, flexitime and working from home make work-life balance easier.
Changing gender roles affect who works and in what jobs, and so change attitudes to work.
notes.tip: Examiners accept any well-explained factors, so name three or four and explain each by saying how it raises or lowers a worker's attitude. A factor that is only named does not earn the marks. Useful ones are family background and upbringing, education, social group, ambition, pay, conditions, personal identity, social contact and gender roles.

notes.h: Variation in attitudes according to occupation
notes.b: Occupations differ in the mix of intrinsic and extrinsic satisfaction they offer, so workers in different jobs often feel differently about their work.
points: Professional and creative occupations, such as teaching, medicine and design, often give high intrinsic satisfaction through responsibility, autonomy and recognised expertise.
Repetitive manual and production jobs, such as assembly-line work, tend to depend more on pay, job security and working conditions, because the task itself offers little interest.
Shift work and unsocial hours can reduce satisfaction in occupations such as nursing, emergency services and hospitality unless flexibility is offered.
Self-employed workers often report high intrinsic satisfaction because they control their own hours and methods, but they bear greater financial risk and have less security.
Occupations that have status in the community encourage a positive attitude to work.
notes.tip: A short question may ask for part-time work for students: give one advantage and one disadvantage, such as earning money, gaining experience and time-management skills against tiredness and less study time.

notes.h: Job descriptions as a starting point
notes.b: A job description sets out what a post involves. In a case study it is the basis for judging how satisfying the work is likely to be.
points: A job description usually states the job title, main duties and responsibilities, working hours, place of work, pay and the qualifications or skills needed.
Duties involving planning, decision-making or creativity suggest scope for intrinsic satisfaction.
Routine, repetitive duties with a fixed pay scale suggest that satisfaction depends mainly on extrinsic rewards.
Flexible hours, job-sharing or home working in a description indicate conditions that can improve work-life balance.
Method: list the duties, mark each as offering intrinsic or extrinsic satisfaction, judge how satisfied the worker is likely to be, then suggest one or two improvements.
notes.tip: In a case study you are given a job description or short profile. Say what satisfaction the worker gets, intrinsic and extrinsic, and then suggest improvements.

notes.b: Satisfaction can be judged by checking both sources of satisfaction and the factors that undermine them. Once the weak points are found, they suggest what to improve.
points: Questions to ask: is the worker paid fairly, is the employment secure, is effort recognised, does the worker use their skills, and is there social contact? Then balance the intrinsic and extrinsic answers.
Variety in tasks, training, more responsibility and clear routes to promotion increase intrinsic satisfaction, because the work becomes more challenging and the worker sees a future.
Taking part in decisions, teamwork and a safe, pleasant workplace raise satisfaction, as do better relationships with management, because the worker feels valued and comfortable.
Fair pay and secure employment improve extrinsic satisfaction, because the worker is rewarded for effort and need not worry about losing the job.
Flexible hours and leave arrangements help workers balance work with family life, so work causes less strain at home.
Regular feedback and recognition reward performance and reinforce commitment, because workers who are told they do well keep up the effort.
notes.tip: For a list question such as three factors that contribute to job satisfaction, use identity and self-esteem, pay and benefits, social contact, working conditions or promotion prospects, and explain each one.

keyTerms.definition: Work done for a wage or salary under a contract with an employer.
Work done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as child care and housework.
Unpaid work done by choice for people outside the household, usually through a charity or community group.
Paid work in which the worker earns income directly from their own trade, business or profession.
A document setting out a post's title, duties, working hours, pay range and required qualifications.
Satisfaction gained from rewards linked to work, such as pay, bonuses and job security, rather than from the task itself.
Satisfaction gained from the work itself, through fulfilment, creativity, challenge and pride.
The attitude a worker brings to work, shown through punctuality, commitment and respect for authority.
The work a person is aiming for, shaped by education, social group, aspirations and opportunity.

factCards.definition: Paid employment; unpaid work in the home and home-related activities; voluntary work.
Pay and bonuses; job security; pension and paid holiday entitlements; company benefits such as a car or private health insurance.
Challenge and variety in tasks; creativity and scope to use skills; pride and sense of achievement; status and respect from the work.
Punctuality; low absenteeism; commitment to tasks; respect for authority and colleagues.

factCards.term: Four factors that shape attitudes to work
factCards.definition: Working conditions; personal identity linked to occupation; social contact and peer pressure; family background and education.

questions.prompt: Distinguish between paid employment and unpaid work in the home, giving one feature of each.
questions.model: Paid employment is done for a wage or salary under a contract with an employer, and carries entitlements such as PRSI-based social insurance, pension and paid holidays. Unpaid work is done without financial reward, mainly in the home, such as child care, housework or caring for an elderly relative. Full marks need a feature for each type, not just a definition.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between extrinsic and intrinsic satisfaction at work. Discuss how each one can shape a worker's attitude to their job, giving an example occupation for each.
questions.model: Extrinsic satisfaction comes from rewards outside the task, such as pay, bonuses, job security and benefits. Intrinsic satisfaction comes from the work itself, such as challenge, creativity, responsibility and pride. Extrinsic rewards can keep a worker committed, especially in repetitive work such as assembly-line production, but they may bring less pride and self-esteem. Intrinsic satisfaction builds self-esteem, confidence and independence, and can give a worker status and a positive attitude to work, as in a professional or creative occupation. Strong intrinsic satisfaction often leads to a better work ethic and higher work attainment.
